# Microsoft Security Control Knowledge Base

Generated from `mock_recommendations.json`, which was pulled live from Microsoft Graph `GET /security/secureScoreControlProfiles?$top=999`. This is a working knowledge base and research plan: every control is indexed, seeded with Microsoft Secure Score remediation data, and assigned a setting-discovery plan/status.

## Research Rules

- Primary truth starts with Microsoft Secure Score / Microsoft Graph data in `mock_recommendations.json`.
- Prefer Microsoft Learn, Microsoft 365 Defender, Microsoft Entra, Exchange, Teams, Purview, Intune, Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity, and Defender for Cloud Apps documentation before third-party pages.
- SaaS controls sourced through Defender for Cloud Apps may require vendor documentation; keep those sources but mark them as non-Microsoft.
- If a setting cannot be confirmed from official documentation, keep the control in the file and mark it as a blocker instead of removing it.
- Never store tenant secrets, tokens, authorization headers, customer user data, or private evidence in this file.

## Microsoft Documentation Enrichment Plan

Goal: enrich every control section with Microsoft-confirmed setting names, required values, and the safest remote-control mechanism. The output of the enrichment pass must stay in this file so Securityzator can later turn the knowledge base into automation lanes.

### Per-Control Target Schema

Each control should eventually contain these subsections after the existing Secure Score seed data:

- Confirmed settings: one row per setting with `Setting`, `Required value`, `Microsoft surface`, `Remote mechanism`, `API/Cmdlet/CSP`, `Required permissions or role`, `License dependency`, `Source`, and `Confidence`.
- Remote control mechanism: one of `Microsoft Graph`, `Intune Graph / Settings Catalog`, `Intune Policy CSP / OMA-URI`, `Exchange Online PowerShell`, `Security & Compliance PowerShell`, `Teams PowerShell`, `SharePoint Online PowerShell`, `Defender XDR / Defender for Endpoint API`, `Hybrid/on-premises action required`, `Vendor/SaaS admin API`, or `Portal/manual only`.
- Blockers: exact reason when no remote mechanism or exact setting can be confirmed from official documentation.

### Official Source Priority

1. Microsoft Graph and Microsoft Learn API docs for the management surface.
2. Microsoft Defender, Intune, Entra, Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, Purview, and Defender for Cloud Apps docs.
3. Microsoft PowerShell module docs when Graph does not expose the setting.
4. Vendor docs only for SaaS controls surfaced through Defender for Cloud Apps.
5. Existing Secure Score remediation text remains a seed, not final proof, unless the action URL itself documents the setting.

### Remote Mechanism Matrix

| Service family | Primary documentation target | Remote-control mechanism to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| Secure Score metadata | Microsoft Graph `secureScoreControlProfiles` docs and Graph Security authorization docs | Read-only collection through `GET /security/secureScoreControlProfiles`; not a configuration mechanism except editable metadata such as tenant notes |
| MDATP / Defender device controls | Defender for Endpoint docs, Intune endpoint security docs, Intune Settings Catalog, Defender Policy CSP | Prefer Intune Graph `deviceManagement/configurationPolicies`; use Policy CSP or OMA-URI when the exact setting is CSP-backed; record Defender API only when Microsoft documents a supported write API |
| Attack Surface Reduction controls | ASR rule reference, ASR deployment docs, Defender Policy CSP | Setting is ASR rule GUID plus mode; remote path is Intune Settings Catalog / Endpoint Security policy or Policy CSP `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/Defender/AttackSurfaceReductionRules` |
| MDO / Exchange Online controls | Microsoft Defender for Office 365 docs and Exchange Online PowerShell docs | Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlets such as `Set-SafeLinksPolicy`, `Set-SafeAttachmentPolicy`, `Set-AntiPhishPolicy`, `Set-HostedContentFilterPolicy`, and corresponding rule cmdlets |
| Entra / AzureAD controls | Microsoft Entra docs and Microsoft Graph identity/policy docs | Microsoft Graph where available: Conditional Access, authorization policy, admin consent request policy, domain password policy, groups, applications, and service principals |
| Azure ATP / Defender for Identity controls | Defender for Identity docs and AD/AD CS hardening docs | Often hybrid/on-premises: AD PowerShell, AD CS tools, GPO, sensor install, or server-side remediation; mark as not safely cloud-remotable unless Microsoft documents an API |
| Teams controls | Teams admin docs and Teams PowerShell docs | Teams PowerShell for meeting policy and tenant-level policy settings unless Microsoft Graph exposes the exact write surface |
| SharePoint / OneDrive / Sway / Forms controls | Microsoft 365 admin, SharePoint admin, Forms/Sway admin, and PowerShell docs | SharePoint Online PowerShell, Microsoft Graph, or portal/manual depending on exact setting |
| MIP / Purview controls | Microsoft Purview and Information Protection docs | Security & Compliance PowerShell or Purview portal/API depending on exact setting |
| Defender for Cloud Apps SaaS controls | Defender for Cloud Apps docs first, then vendor docs | Usually vendor/SaaS admin setting; record Defender for Cloud Apps as discovery/recommendation source, not automatic enforcement, unless a vendor API is documented |

### Execution Order

1. MDATP device controls: highest count and many share repeatable ASR, Defender AV, firewall, SmartScreen, BitLocker, and Windows security baseline surfaces.
2. Azure ATP / Defender for Identity controls: classify which are cloud-readable versus hybrid/on-premises remediations.
3. MDO and EXO controls: map Defender for Office settings to Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlets and portal settings.
4. AzureAD / Entra controls: map Conditional Access, authorization, consent, group, app, password, and admin-account controls to Microsoft Graph or portal-only mechanisms.
5. Teams, SPO, MIP, Forms, Sway, and Admincenter controls: map smaller Microsoft 365 workloads.
6. MDA SaaS controls: preserve Microsoft Secure Score context, then confirm vendor setting names and whether a remote API exists.

### Milestone M1 Progress - MDATP ASR Rules

Status: 19 MDATP controls are confirmed as Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules. Microsoft documents the rule names, GUIDs, modes, and management surfaces. These controls share the same enforceable setting shape.

Confirmed common setting:

| Setting | Required value | Microsoft surface | Remote mechanism | API/Cmdlet/CSP | Permissions or role | License dependency | Sources | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attack Surface Reduction rule state | `1` / `Block` for each listed ASR rule GUID | Microsoft Intune Endpoint Security / Attack surface reduction, Settings Catalog, or custom OMA-URI profile | Automatable through Intune Graph / Settings Catalog; semi-automatable through Policy CSP / OMA-URI; local PowerShell fallback exists but is not durable if Intune or another device-management plane owns policy | `POST /deviceManagement/configurationPolicies`; CSP path `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/Defender/AttackSurfaceReductionRules`; value format `GUID=1` or pipe-delimited `GUID=StateValue` list | Application permission `DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All` or `DeviceManagementEndpointSecurity.ReadWrite.All` for Graph writes; Intune administrator or equivalent role for portal changes | Active Intune license for Intune Graph policy writes; Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 applies to the ASR reference page | Microsoft ASR reference; Enable ASR rules; Defender Policy CSP; Intune configuration policy Graph docs | High |

Microsoft ASR mode values:

| Mode | Value | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| Off / disabled | `0` | Rule is not applied |
| Block | `1` | Rule is enforced |
| Audit | `2` | Rule is evaluated and logged but not enforced |
| Not configured | `5` | Rule uses default behavior |
| Warn | `6` | Rule is enforced but user can bypass where supported |

M1 ASR blockers and implementation notes:

- `scid_2507` has a Microsoft-documented Intune ASR policy backend availability caveat; use CSP, Defender for Endpoint security settings management, PowerShell, or existing Intune ASR policies if the Settings Catalog path is unavailable.
- Policy conflicts can occur when multiple device management planes configure ASR; Microsoft documents that Intune, Configuration Manager, or another enterprise management tool can overwrite local Group Policy or PowerShell settings.
- ASR exclusions use separate CSP path `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/Defender/AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions`; exclusions are not the secure target and should be modeled as an exception workflow, not baseline enforcement.

### Milestone M1 Progress - Core Windows Defender, Firewall, SmartScreen, BitLocker, and EDR

Status: 27 additional MDATP controls have been mapped into confirmed Microsoft management surfaces or explicit blocker classes. This batch covers Defender Antivirus, network protection, cloud protection, tamper protection, SmartScreen, Microsoft Defender Firewall, BitLocker, Defender for Endpoint onboarding/health, and EDR in block mode.

| Intune endpoint security and Settings Catalog | Microsoft Graph write to Intune configuration policy | `POST /deviceManagement/configurationPolicies` plus assignments | `DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All` or `DeviceManagementEndpointSecurity.ReadWrite.All`; Intune admin role | Preferred path when the setting is exposed in endpoint security or Settings Catalog. |
| Policy CSP / OMA-URI | Intune custom device configuration or Settings Catalog-backed CSP | CSP path under `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/...` | Same Intune Graph permissions for policy writes | Use when Microsoft documents a CSP but the friendly Intune setting template is gated, renamed, or not available. |

Defender Antivirus notes and blockers:

- `scid_2010` ("Turn on Microsoft Defender Antivirus") is a device health/control-state recommendation, not one single safe policy toggle. Model it as a composite of Defender service health plus `AllowRealtimeMonitoring=1`, `AllowOnAccessProtection=1`, cloud protection, platform/signature freshness, and MDE onboarding status.
- `scid_2011` ("Update Microsoft Defender Antivirus definitions") maps to security intelligence update state. Microsoft documents `SignatureUpdateInterval` as a configurable check interval from `0-24` hours and `Update-MpSignature` as local remediation, but Secure Score's exact freshness threshold should be confirmed from the live recommendation details before hardcoding a pass/fail value.
- `scid_2014` ("Fix Windows Defender Antivirus cloud service connectivity") is primarily network/proxy allow-list remediation. It should become a diagnostic/remediation workflow that validates Defender AV cloud endpoints rather than a normal settings-catalog toggle.
- Tamper protection can prevent changes to several Defender settings. If Securityzator changes Defender AV settings remotely, it should detect tamper-protected setting conflict and surface a dependency message instead of repeatedly writing a policy that will not apply.

Firewall blockers and implementation notes:

- The Microsoft firewall docs confirm the relevant knobs, but the exact Secure Score scoring bundle for "secure profile" should be verified against the live recommendation details before Securityzator silently disables all local firewall rule merge behavior.
- Firewall rule deployment has an all-or-nothing behavior on modern Windows Atomic blocks. Securityzator should validate each generated firewall rule before assignment and should avoid mixing unrelated firewall rules into the same profile.

M1 core Windows blockers and implementation notes:

- `scid_2004` has an M1.8 source pass in the individual section. Before Securityzator writes `PassiveRemediation`, stage a pilot device group and validate policy result because `0x1` enables Sense AutoRemediation and additional flags (`0x2`, `0x4`) change real-time protection remediation behavior.
- `scid_2001`, `scid_2002`, `scid_2014`, `scid_2091`, and `scid_2093` are repair/health recommendations. They should become diagnostic workflows with evidence collection and a remediation action, not simple persistent configuration settings.
- `scid_2080` ("Turn on Microsoft Defender Credential Guard") and `scid_2020` ("Turn on all system-level Exploit protection settings") now have an M1 source pass below. Credential Guard is a high-confidence DeviceGuard CSP mapping; Exploit Protection is confirmed as XML policy deployment but needs a tenant-approved XML artifact before automation can enforce it.

### Milestone M1 Progress - Credential Guard, Exploit Protection, Secure Launch, and Secure Boot

Status: 4 more MDATP controls have been classified. Credential Guard and Exploit Protection are automatable through Intune/MDM with clear CSP-backed surfaces. Secure Launch is automatable when hardware supports it. Secure Boot is best modeled as posture/compliance plus manual/OEM remediation, because MDM can require/report it but cannot reliably flip firmware mode on arbitrary hardware.

Confirmed controls:

| Control ID | Secure Score title | Confirmed setting or state | Required value | Remote mechanism | Source confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `scid_2080` | Turn on Microsoft Defender Credential Guard | Device Guard VBS plus Credential Guard configuration | `EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity=1`; `LsaCfgFlags=2` for enabled without UEFI lock, or `1` for enabled with UEFI lock | Intune Settings Catalog or custom CSP: `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/DeviceGuard/EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity` and `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/DeviceGuard/LsaCfgFlags` | High |
| `scid_2020` | Turn on all system-level Exploit protection settings | Exploit protection mitigation policy XML | Upload/export XML containing the tenant-approved system-level mitigations; deploy through `ExploitProtectionSettings` | Intune Endpoint Security Attack Surface Reduction / Exploit Protection profile, Configuration Manager, Group Policy, PowerShell, or `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/ExploitGuard/ExploitProtectionSettings` | Medium-high |
| `scid_112` | Ensure devices are updated to Secure Boot 2023 certificates and boot manager | Secure Boot certificate/update state | Do not opt out of high-confidence Secure Boot certificate update buckets; keep monthly cumulative update path healthy | Windows update posture plus SecureBoot Policy CSP `ConfigureHighConfidenceOptOut=0` | Medium |
| `scid_2100` | Enable UEFI Secure Boot mode | Secure Boot enabled and health-attested device posture | `Confirm-SecureBootUEFI` returns `True`; Intune compliance can require Secure Boot | Compliance policy / device health attestation for detection; firmware/OEM/manual remediation if disabled or unsupported | Medium |

Credential Guard implementation notes:

- Prefer `LsaCfgFlags=2` ("enabled without lock") for Securityzator automation because Microsoft warns that UEFI lock can require physical presence to undo.
- Enabling Credential Guard requires a restart and should ideally happen before domain join or before domain users first sign in.
- Verification should use `Win32_DeviceGuard.SecurityServicesRunning`, System Information, or Event Viewer; Microsoft explicitly says checking `LsaIso.exe` in Task Manager is not the preferred proof.

Exploit Protection implementation notes:

- The setting payload is XML, not a scalar. Securityzator should store the approved XML template separately, hash it, and reference its version in the knowledge base or automation plan.
- "All system-level Exploit protection settings" should not be blindly inferred from the generic Microsoft example XML. Use a tenant-approved Windows Security Baseline, export from a reference device, or import Microsoft baseline content, then deploy through Intune.
- Audit mode is supported and should be a rollout option before enforcing high-impact mitigations.

Secure Boot and Secure Launch cautions:

- `scid_2100` is not safely remediated as a remote switch. Firmware mode, UEFI support, TPM/PCR7 binding, and OEM settings determine whether Secure Boot can be enabled.
- `scid_112` is remediable as a staged SecureBoot certificate/update workflow, but it still depends on Windows update/Secure Boot rollout state and recovery-media readiness. The secure posture is to leave `ConfigureHighConfidenceOptOut=0`, enable certificate updates only when prepared, and keep update channels healthy.
- Secure Launch uses `DeviceGuard/ConfigureSystemGuardLaunch=1`, but Microsoft documents hardware prerequisites. Treat failures as eligibility/remediation issues, not simple policy failures.

Most map to Microsoft Policy CSP through Intune Settings Catalog or custom OMA-URI. Items that require domain controller policy, app compatibility validation, or device-local remediation are marked as confirmed staged workflows or blockers rather than treated as simple toggles.

M1.4 implementation notes:

- Account policy controls affect local accounts through DeviceLock/MDM; domain account password policy still belongs to Active Directory or Entra policy surfaces. Securityzator should label scope clearly before applying.
- ADMX-backed CSP rows should not store raw encoded SyncML in this knowledge base. Store the human setting and required value here; generate and version the SyncML payload in the automation layer.
- LDAP and NTLM controls are high-impact. Securityzator should implement an `audit -> report affected apps/devices -> staged enforce` workflow rather than one-click blocking.
- SMBv1, WDigest, and Remote Registry are excellent candidates for Intune remediation scripts with before/after evidence capture because they are operational state fixes more than durable tenant settings.

### Milestone M1.5 Progress - Microsoft Defender Firewall Details

Status: 5 MDATP controls were confirmed against the Microsoft Firewall CSP and Intune endpoint security Firewall documentation. These are profile-level firewall settings, not custom firewall rules. All five depend on the relevant profile's firewall being enabled before the CSP value is meaningful.

Common remote-control pattern:

| Surface | Automatable path | Graph/API object | Permission or role | Notes |

| Group Policy / local firewall policy | GPO or local PowerShell fallback | Windows Firewall with Advanced Security policy store | Domain/GPO admin or local admin | Useful for unmanaged or hybrid devices, but Securityzator should prefer the same cloud policy owner across a device fleet. |

M1.5 implementation notes:

- Microsoft documents the `DisableInboundNotifications`, `AllowLocalPolicyMerge`, and `AllowLocalIpsecPolicyMerge` nodes as `Get, Replace` Firewall CSP values, so they are safe to model as durable policy settings rather than device-health remediations.
- The public-profile rule-merge settings can intentionally override locally created firewall and IPsec rules. Securityzator should warn before enforcement and should inventory known local exceptions for VPN, remote support, EDR, and line-of-business agents.
- This pass confirms the five explicit Secure Score firewall-detail controls. The broader profile controls `scid_2071`, `scid_2072`, and `scid_2073` remain medium-high until the full Secure Score bundle is validated against live recommendation evidence.

- Office update controls are Microsoft-owned and can be safely modeled as durable Office ADMX policy. Use `EnableAutomaticUpdates=1` and `HideEnableDisableUpdates=1` under `HKLM\software\policies\microsoft\office\16.0\common\OfficeUpdate` for Microsoft 365 Apps / Office 2016+.
- Chrome removed the old plugin/Flash policies. Securityzator should not attempt to enforce removed Chrome settings on current Chrome; instead, report these as retired-policy blockers and use current browser version/update posture as the real remediation lane.
- Chrome Autofill was split into address and credit-card policies. Use both current policies for enforcement, but validate whether Defender TVM still scores the deprecated `AutoFillEnabled` registry value before marking the Secure Score item remediated.
- Adobe JavaScript and Flash controls are registry lockdowns, not Graph-native tenant settings. Model them as remediation scripts with before/after evidence and version/product detection for `Acrobat Reader` versus `Adobe Acrobat`.
- Office Flash activation is available through the Microsoft 365 Apps security baseline and `MS Security Guide` ADMX. Prefer the Intune baseline/Settings Catalog surface when possible; avoid hand-writing the tattooing registry values unless policy import is not available.
- Internet Explorer ActiveX posture is legacy. Keep blocking enabled, do not allow exceptions broadly, and treat Trusted Sites / Local Intranet bypasses as a separate allow-list governance workflow.

M1.7 implementation notes:

- Microsoft cleanly documents Defender settings for macOS and Linux, but not every Secure Score host-hardening control has a first-party remote write surface. Treat those as blockers or manual/hybrid workflows rather than inventing fake automation.
- For macOS passcode settings, Intune documents the exact controls for minimum length, password age, password history, and maximum sign-in attempts. These are close matches for Secure Score, but they still depend on enrollment type and Apple platform behavior.
- SIP, home folder permissions, and unrestricted Linux access accounts should become separate host-hardening workflows with detection evidence, not one-click MDM toggles.
- Definitions freshness recommendations should combine durable settings with an operational remediation action. Policy should keep automatic updates enabled; remediation should still be able to invoke `mdatp definitions update` or package-manager upgrade when devices drift.
- Health/connectivity recommendations for both macOS and Linux should capture `mdatp health`, `mdatp connectivity test`, and `mdatp diagnostic create` output before and after remediation so Securityzator can preserve evidence instead of just flipping a status.

### Milestone M1.8 Progress - Windows File Share, LDAP/NTLM, Remote Registry, and Secure Boot Residue

Status: 20 late-list and adjacent MDATP controls have been mapped to Microsoft-documented settings or explicit staged-remediation blockers. The file-share controls are operational SMB share remediations, service-path controls are device-local service configuration repairs, `scid_2030` is a Windows Server legacy Defender for Endpoint agent migration item, EDR in block mode is confirmed through Defender portal/CSP surfaces, built-in Administrator/Guest controls map to LocalPoliciesSecurityOptions CSP, LDAP/NTLM controls need audit-first rollout, Remote Registry is a device-local service remediation, and Secure Boot controls are posture/update controls with firmware caveats.

Confirmed and classified M1.8 controls:

| Control ID | Secure Score title | Classification | Confirmed setting or state | Required value | Remote mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `scid_45` | Set user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication to 'Enabled' | Confirmed | ADMX Terminal Server `TS_USER_AUTHENTICATION_POLICY` | Enabled; registry posture `UserAuthentication=1` | Intune Administrative Templates / Settings Catalog / ADMX-backed CSP |
| `scid_4000` | Disallow offline access to shares | Confirmed remediation | SMB share `CachingMode` | `None` | PowerShell / CIM / Intune remediation: `Set-SmbShare -CachingMode None` |
| `scid_4001` | Remove share write permission set to 'Everyone' | Confirmed remediation | SMB share ACL has no `Everyone` allow ACE with `Change` or `Full` | Remove `Everyone` write-capable ACE; replace with least-privilege groups | PowerShell / CIM / Intune remediation: `Get-SmbShareAccess`, `Revoke-SmbShareAccess`, `Grant-SmbShareAccess` |
| `scid_4002` | Remove shares from the root folder | Confirmed remediation | Non-admin SMB shares do not expose a drive root such as `C:\` or `D:\` | Remove or relocate root-path shares; preserve built-in administrative shares as separate exception class | PowerShell / CIM / Intune remediation: `Get-SmbShare`, `Remove-SmbShare`, `New-SmbShare` |
| `scid_4003` | Set folder access-based enumeration for shares | Confirmed remediation | SMB share `FolderEnumerationMode` | `AccessBased` | PowerShell / CIM / Intune remediation: `Set-SmbShare -FolderEnumerationMode AccessBased` |
| `scid_2030` | Update Microsoft Defender for Endpoint core components | Confirmed migration | Legacy Windows Server 2012 R2/2016 MDE/MMA machines moved to current unified solution | Install/upgrade unified Defender for Endpoint package and apply onboarding script | Defender portal package, migration script, Configuration Manager, Defender for Cloud, or software distribution |
| `scid_3001` | Fix unquoted service path for Windows services | Confirmed remediation | Windows service `PathName` / service `binpath` has a quoted executable path when the path contains spaces | Quote the executable path while preserving service arguments | Intune remediation / PowerShell / RMM / `sc.exe config` |
| `scid_3002` | Change service executable path to a common protected location | Confirmed remediation | Service executable resolves to an absolute path in a non-user-writable protected directory | Move/reinstall service binary under an admin-writable-only location such as vendor install path, `Program Files`, or `Windows`; update service path after testing | Vendor repair/reinstall preferred; PowerShell / RMM / `sc.exe config` when supported |
| `scid_3003` | Change service account to avoid cached password in windows registry | Confirmed remediation | Service `StartName` does not use a normal local/domain user password where a managed/virtual/built-in account is supported | Prefer gMSA/sMSA, virtual service account, `LocalService`, `NetworkService`, or approved `LocalSystem` instead of a password-backed user account | AD gMSA provisioning plus service reconfiguration; PowerShell / RMM / `sc.exe config obj=` |
| `scid_2004` | Enable EDR in block mode | Confirmed | Defender portal advanced feature or Defender CSP `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Defender/Configuration/PassiveRemediation` | Tenant-wide portal toggle enabled, or targeted CSP value includes `0x1` Sense AutoRemediation | Defender portal, Intune custom CSP, or GPO |
| `scid_3010` | Disable the built-in Administrator account | Confirmed | `LocalPoliciesSecurityOptions/Accounts_EnableAdministratorAccountStatus` | `0` / disabled | Intune Settings Catalog / custom OMA-URI / GPO / local remediation |
| `scid_3011` | Disable the built-in Guest account | Confirmed | `LocalPoliciesSecurityOptions/Accounts_EnableGuestAccountStatus` | `0` / disabled | Intune Settings Catalog / custom OMA-URI / GPO / local remediation |
| `scid_102` | Enable 'Local Security Authority (LSA) protection' on Windows 11 22h2 and higher | Confirmed | `LocalSecurityAuthority/ConfigureLsaProtectedProcess` | `2` enabled without UEFI lock for reversible automation; `1` with UEFI lock for stricter tenants | Intune Settings Catalog / custom OMA-URI |
| `scid_103` | Require LDAP client signing to prevent tampering and protect directory authentication | Confirmed with OS caveat | `LocalPoliciesSecurityOptions/NetworkSecurity_LDAPClientSigningRequirements` | `2` / require signing | Intune Settings Catalog / LocalPoliciesSecurityOptions CSP on supported OS; GPO otherwise |
| `scid_104` | Encrypt LDAP client traffic to protect sensitive data in transit | Blocker | LDAP clients use LDAPS/TLS or SASL signing/sealing | No universal client toggle confirmed | App/client remediation, directory TLS validation, and compatibility inventory |
| `scid_105` | Enforce LDAP channel binding to protect authentication sessions from interception | Hybrid blocker | Domain controller LDAP channel binding enforcement | `LdapEnforceChannelBinding=2` after audit where compatible | Domain Controller GPO/registry with staged rollout |
| `scid_106` | Require LDAP server signing to ensure integrity of directory traffic | Hybrid blocker | Domain controller LDAP server signing | `LDAPServerIntegrity=2` after client readiness | Domain Controller GPO/registry with staged rollout |

M1.8 implementation notes:

- File-share controls should be implemented as detect-plan-apply workflows with before/after share inventory because removing or changing shares can disconnect users and cause data-loss risk if active sessions exist.
- Service-path controls should be implemented as evidence-backed repairs: parse the executable and arguments separately, preserve vendor service arguments, prefer vendor reinstall/repair for path relocation, and never move a running service binary without a rollback plan.
- Service-account remediation should prefer managed or virtual identities and must not collect, log, or store service account passwords. Built-in Administrator disablement needs a verified alternate local admin or LAPS/break-glass path before enforcement.
- LDAP and NTLM controls are audit-first by design. Securityzator should surface affected apps, devices, and domain controllers before offering enforcement.
- Remote Registry is a simple service-state remediation technically, but it can break legacy assessment, inventory, or management tooling. Treat it as low-complexity/high-compatibility-risk.
- Secure Boot 2023 certificate controls are moving target update posture. Prefer the supported SecureBoot CSP values and Windows Update evidence over raw registry toggling except in an explicit break-glass/remediation workflow.

SSPR, LinkedIn, and Sway are confirmed admin-center settings that should remain portal-first until a current Microsoft write API is explicitly confirmed. M4.2 implementation notes:

- Consent and app-registration controls must preserve existing non-user consent policy assignments when patching `authorizationPolicy`; read current policy first, then apply the minimal delta.
- Conditional Access controls should always be created in report-only mode first and must exclude validated emergency access accounts to avoid tenant lockout.
- SSPR and custom banned-password controls are easy to express but not equally easy to automate from a stable public write API; Securityzator should model them as guided actions until Microsoft documents a supported automation path.
- Defender for Cloud Apps enablement is a readiness/onboarding workflow, not a single setting. Evidence should capture license/portal access, connected apps, discovery ingestion, and active policies.
- On-premises password protection is hybrid and requires server deployment, restart planning, event-log monitoring, and an audit-to-enforced transition.

M2.1 implementation notes:

- Defender for Identity security assessments update near real time for exposed entities, but Secure Score status can lag up to 24 hours. Securityzator should capture before/after evidence instead of waiting synchronously on the score.
- AD CS changes can break certificate enrollment and authentication. Require backup/export, owner approval, and a controlled rollout before changing templates or CA publication.
- Honeytoken accounts should be deliberately attractive but unused; any authentication or directory probing against them should be treated as an alerting signal.
- VPN integration currently depends on Defender for Identity sensor v2.x and RADIUS accounting. Sensor v3.x support limitations matter for future rollout planning.
- Privileged-account and service-account remediations must be dependency-aware. Remove standing privileges only after owner review, last-logon/dependency checks, and a rollback path.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| `AATP_AzureSsoAccountOldPasswords` | Change password for Entra seamless SSO account | Confirmed hybrid identity remediation | `AZUREADSSOACC` Kerberos decryption key rolled over | Roll over at least every 30 days; Defender finding clears for accounts older than 90 days | Microsoft Entra Connect PowerShell / Seamless SSO key rollover |
| `AATP_BuiltinKrbtgtAccountWithOldPassword` | Change password for krbtgt account | Confirmed AD DS remediation | KRBTGT password rotated safely | Reset twice, waiting at least 10 hours between resets | AD DS KRBTGT reset procedure |
| `AATP_AdAccountWithPotentiallyLeakedCredentials` | Change password for on-prem account with potentially leaked credentials | Confirmed incident remediation | Affected on-prem AD account password changed and sessions/risk reviewed | Reset password; revoke sessions where applicable; investigate source | ADUC / AD PowerShell / Defender for Identity exposed entities |
| `AATP_BuiltinAdministratorAccountWithOldPassword` | Change password of built-in domain Administrator account | Confirmed AD DS remediation | Built-in domain Administrator password rotated | Reset stale built-in Administrator password and monitor usage | ADUC / AD PowerShell / privileged account governance |
| `AATP_ADCSInsecureCertificateEnrollmentIisEndpoints` | Edit insecure certificate enrollment IIS endpoints (ESC8) | Confirmed AD CS / IIS remediation | Certificate enrollment IIS endpoints do not expose NTLM relay risk | Disable unused endpoints; disable NTLM/Negotiate or require SSL plus Extended Protection | IIS / AD CS web enrollment configuration |
| `AATP_ADCSMisconfiguredCertificateAuthorityAcl` | Edit misconfigured Certificate Authority ACL (ESC7) | Confirmed AD CS remediation | CA ACL does not grant unprivileged `Manage CA` or `Manage Certificates` rights | Remove broad/built-in unprivileged permissions from CA ACL | Certification Authority console / AD CS permissions |
| `AATP_ADCSMisconfiguredCertificateTemplateAcl` | Edit misconfigured certificate templates ACL (ESC4) | Confirmed AD CS remediation | Template ACL does not grant unprivileged template-modification rights | Remove Full Control, Write DACL, Write Owner, Write Property, or equivalent broad permissions | Certificate Templates MMC / AD object ACLs |
| `AATP_ADCSMisconfiguredCertificateTemplateOwner` | Edit misconfigured certificate templates owner (ESC4) | Confirmed AD CS remediation | Template owner is privileged and monitored | Change owner away from unprivileged/broad principals | Certificate Templates MMC / AD object owner |
| `AATP_ADCSMisconfiguredCertificateTemplateEnrollmentAgent` | Edit misconfigured enrollment agent certificate template (ESC3) | Confirmed AD CS remediation | Enrollment Agent templates cannot be abused by unprivileged users | Remove Certificate Request Agent EKU, restrict enrollment, require manager approval/signatures, or unpublish template | Certificate Templates MMC / CA enrollment agent restrictions |

M2.2 implementation notes:

- Password-age remediations need sequencing. KRBTGT requires two resets with a delay; Seamless SSO key rollover must not be run more than once per forest in a short window.
- AD CS remediations are high-impact. Always export template/CA configuration, identify dependent services, and test in a controlled environment before enforcement.
- Insecure IIS enrollment endpoints are an ESC8 relay path. If the endpoint is not needed, disabling it is safer than trying to compensate with TLS/EPA.
- Leaked credential and built-in Administrator password remediations should include session review, sign-in review, and privileged account monitoring, not just a password reset.

- Sensor controls are deployment coverage items, not cloud toggles. They need server installation, service validation, auditing prerequisites, and Defender XDR sensor inventory review.
- GPO and delegation changes should be staged with owner review. Both can break legacy delegation or endpoint-local admin workflows if remediated blindly.

- Several controls are evidence-guided rather than one-click automations: Defender XDR identifies exposed entities, but remediation happens in AD DS, GPO, Entra Connect, host local admin membership, or dependency-managed service-account workflows.

- Stale user and service account cleanup needs a staged disable/monitor/delete path. That is especially true for service accounts, where "no recent logon" can still hide fragile legacy jobs.

- The Print Spooler recommendation has an explicit operational tradeoff: disabling it on DCs reduces credential exposure risk, but print pruning may need a replacement operational process.

B10.5 implementation notes:

- Salesforce public Help pages are sometimes difficult to scrape directly, but Microsoft Secure Score remediation text, Salesforce Help search snippets, Salesforce Well-Architected guidance, and the Salesforce metadata surface all align on the same Session Settings / Login Access Policies controls.
- These controls are good connector candidates: read `Settings/Security` metadata, inspect `SecuritySettings` and `SessionSettings`, then deploy a targeted metadata update. Use a Salesforce integration principal with metadata permissions and change-control safeguards.
- Clickjack, CSRF, content sniffing, and CSP changes can affect custom Visualforce, embedded pages, legacy integrations, and email-template behavior. Securityzator should recommend sandbox validation before production deployment.
- For `Administrators Can Log In As Any User`, disabling the org-wide bypass does not remove troubleshooting entirely; it restores user-granted login access and preserves stronger privacy/audit boundaries.

This pass covers history, lockout duration, invalid attempts, length, secret-answer handling, complexity, password-question restriction, minimum lifetime, session timeout, and password expiration.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| `MDA_SF_password_lockoutInterval` | Lockout effective period | Confirmed Salesforce lockout policy | Locked-out users remain locked for at least 30 minutes | `passwordPolicies.lockoutInterval=ThirtyMinutes`, `SixtyMinutes`, or `Forever` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_maxLoginAttempts` | Maximum invalid login attempts | Confirmed Salesforce lockout policy | Account lockout after 3 invalid attempts | `passwordPolicies.maxLoginAttempts=ThreeAttempts` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_password_minimumPasswordLength` | Minimum password length | Confirmed Salesforce password policy | Minimum password length is 8 or more | `passwordPolicies.minimumPasswordLength >= 8` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_password_obscureSecretAnswer` | Obscure secret answer for password resets | Confirmed Salesforce password-reset policy | Secret answer is obscured | `passwordPolicies.obscureSecretAnswer=true` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_password_complexity` | Password complexity requirement | Confirmed Salesforce password policy | Passwords require alpha, numeric, and special characters or stronger | `passwordPolicies.complexity=SpecialCharacters`, `UpperLowerCaseNumericSpecialCharacters`, or `Any3UpperLowerCaseNumericSpecialCharacters` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_password_questionRestriction` | Password question requirement | Confirmed Salesforce password-reset policy | Password question answer cannot contain password | `passwordPolicies.questionRestriction=DoesNotContainPassword` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_minimumPasswordLifetime` | Require a minimum 1 day password lifetime | Confirmed Salesforce password policy | Users cannot immediately churn passwords to bypass history | `passwordPolicies.minimumPasswordLifetime=true` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_password_sessionTimeout` | Session timeout | Confirmed Salesforce session policy | Inactive session timeout is 2 hours or less | `sessionSettings.sessionTimeout` in `FifteenMinutes`, `ThirtyMinutes`, `SixtyMinutes`, or `TwoHours` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |
| `MDA_SF_password_expiration` | User passwords expire in 90 days or less | Confirmed Salesforce password policy | Password expiration is 90 days or less | `passwordPolicies.expiration=NinetyDays`, `SixtyDays`, or `ThirtyDays` | Salesforce Setup / Metadata API `Settings/Security` |

B10.6 implementation notes:

- Salesforce Password Policies can exist at org level and, in some orgs, profile-specific password policies can override the org-level baseline. Securityzator should read org `SecuritySettings` first, then profile password policies where present before declaring tenant-wide compliance.
- Some controls have "or stronger" semantics. For example, `ThirtyMinutes`, `SixtyMinutes`, and `Forever` satisfy the lockout-duration control, while `TwoHours` or shorter satisfies session timeout.
- Salesforce notes SSO authorities usually handle lockout for users with SSO enabled. Still, Salesforce password-policy controls matter for direct-login users, break-glass admins, API/security-token edge cases, and any user not fully governed by the IdP.
- Metadata writes are feasible but should be treated as change-controlled deployments. Password/session changes can affect integrations, support flows, and user experience, so staged/sandbox validation remains the safe path.

B10.8 implementation notes:

- Zoom controls are official portal settings. Some Zoom settings are exposed through account settings APIs, but the support docs are the durable source here; model API writes as tenant-validated automation rather than guaranteed universal support.
- Zoom domain blocking only works when participants authenticate; the official docs say the domain block list must be used with authentication profiles. Securityzator should warn when a tenant enables the block list without requiring authentication.
- Zoom E2EE has real tradeoffs: web app, telephone, and SIP/H.323 participants are not supported, and several meeting features are disabled. This is a strong privacy mode, not a frictionless default for every business workflow.
- Okta policy evaluation is rule-priority based. Checking only the default policy is insufficient if higher-priority group policies override the baseline.
- Okta password policies apply to Okta and AD/LDAP-sourced users according to source-specific behavior. For AD/LDAP users, compare Okta policy with the upstream directory policy before claiming full enforcement.

| `AATP_Okta_SensitiveApiToken` | Highly Privileged Okta Api Token | Confirmed Okta token-governance control | Privileged Okta API tokens inventoried and unused/unapproved tokens removed | No unused/unapproved privileged API tokens | Okta API Tokens API and token admin workflow |
| `AATP_Okta_HighNumberOfSuperAdmins` | Limit the Number of Okta Super Admins Accounts | Confirmed Okta super-admin governance control | Super Administrator assignments minimized | Only approved break-glass/core operators retain `SUPER_ADMIN` | Okta Roles API and admin-role review |
| `AATP_Okta_Dormant` | Remove dormant Okta privileged accounts | Confirmed Okta dormant privileged-account control | Dormant privileged admins removed, deactivated, or role-stripped | All exposed dormant privileged accounts remediated | Okta Users API, Roles API, and admin workflow |
| `McasFirewallLogUpload` | Deploy a log collector to discover shadow IT activity | Confirmed Defender for Cloud Apps Cloud Discovery control | Automatic log upload configured with data source and log collector | At least one active data source/log collector continuously uploading firewall/proxy logs | Defender XDR portal guided workflow and log collector health |
| `dlp_datalossprevention` | Ensure DLP policies are enabled | Confirmed Microsoft Purview DLP control | At least one Microsoft 365 DLP policy exists and is enabled/deployed | One or more enabled DLP compliance policies | Purview portal and Security & Compliance PowerShell |

B10.13 implementation notes:

- Okta controls are Microsoft posture findings over third-party identity data. Securityzator should treat Microsoft as the detector and Okta as the remediation/readback plane.
- Okta API tokens inherit the permissions of the creating user and are valid only while that user remains active. Privileged token hygiene must join token metadata to the creator's user and role assignments.
- Dormant/old-password Okta controls are exposed-entity remediations. A tenant should not be scored as remediated until every exposed privileged entity is resolved, not merely until a policy exists.
- Defender for Cloud Apps log collector rollout is infrastructure work, not just a portal toggle. Health checks must include data source, collector status, and recent uploaded traffic logs.
- Purview DLP should start in audit/low-impact mode when appropriate, but Secure Score's baseline requirement is the existence of at least one Microsoft 365 DLP policy.

- ADMX-backed CSP rows should continue to store the friendly policy intent and required state here. Securityzator should generate and test the SyncML payload in the automation layer.
- SMBv1 changes can break legacy file sharing and may require restart when using optional-feature or service-dependency remediation. Capture before/after state and warn on legacy dependency evidence.
- UAC remote restrictions are secure when filtered-token behavior is active. Treat `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy=1` as a finding because it gives local administrator accounts elevated remote tokens.
- Network Bridge and ICS controls are location/domain aware. Securityzator should label these as device policy with DNS-domain scope rather than universal network-state enforcement.
- Remote Assistance and AlwaysInstallElevated are low-noise high-value closures: they have clear device/user policy surfaces and good validation signals.

Follow these steps to create a Conditional Access policy from scratch or by using a template If you would like to perform the implementation yourself and you’re using Microsoft Entra ID Free, turn on security defaults. Note: Security defaults and Conditional Access can’t be used side by side. Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- In order to enable SSO authentication in Workplace you will need to:
- Have access to your Identity Provider's configuration settings. Have a System Administrator role assigned in Workplace. Have a corresponding account in the Identity Provider with the same email as the Workplace user you are logged in with (i.e. which uses the same email address to authenticate both in Workplace and in the Identity Provider). This is essential to test SSO and complete Workplace configuration correctly.    In the Admin Panel, select Security. Click on the Authentication tab. Check the Single Sign-On (SSO) checkbox. Click +Add New SSO Provider. Type in the values provided by your Identity Provider into the relevant fields: SAML URL, SAML Issuer URL, SAML Logout Redirect (Optional), SAML Certificate. Scroll to the bottom of the section and click the Test SSO button. This will result in a popup window appearing with your Identity Provider login page presented. Enter your credentials to authenticate. Once the test has been completed successfully, scroll to the bottom of the page and click Save button. If required, Configure SSO as the default authentication for new users by selecting SSO in the Default to new users drop-down.  To comply with the control, the adoption rate must be above 80%.

Implementation notes:

- For historical posture, preserve SSO evidence and adoption percentage. For current operations, treat migration/export/decommission as the secure end state.
- If a customer still has read-only Workplace access, score the old control only from evidence and do not attempt destructive changes.

- Go to Security > Multifactor panel. Go to "Factor Enrollment" and select "Add Multifactor Policy". Note: In order to comply, you must configure default policies as "required" ("optional" is not sufficient).

- Control ID: `mdo_blockmailforward`

- Research status: B10.16 confirmed from Microsoft external forwarding, outbound spam policy, remote-domain, mailbox-forwarding, and transport-rule documentation.
- Confidence: High for the outbound anti-spam control; medium-high for the composite playbook because "all forms" requires coordinated discovery across several Exchange forwarding paths.

Confirmed setting candidates:

- Outbound spam policy automatic forwarding is set to `Off` for strongest posture, or `Automatic` if the organization deliberately accepts Microsoft system-controlled behavior.
- Remote domains do not permit external automatic forwarding unless an approved exception exists.
- Existing transport rules that redirect mail externally are removed, disabled, or exception-scoped.
- Mailbox forwarding and inbox-rule forwarding are discovered and remediated separately because Microsoft documents several automatic forwarding mechanisms.

Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- NOTE: In this control, remediation is carried out in two stages - Step 1 is manual and will not be monitored automatically by secure score, whereas Step 2 is monitored automatically:
- STEP 1: Transport rules
- To alter the mail transport rules so they do not forward email to external domains, use the Microsoft 365 Admin Center:
- Select Exchange to open the Exchange admin center. Select Mail Flow then Rules. For each rule that redirects email to external domains, select the rule and click the 'Delete' icon.  To perform remediation you may also use the Exchange Online PowerShell
- Module:
- Connect to Exchange Online user Connect-ExchangeOnline. Run the following PowerShell command:
- Remove-TransportRule {RuleName}
- To verify this worked you may re-run the audit command as follows:
- Get-TransportRule | Where-Object {$_.RedirectMessageTo -ne $null} | ft
- Name,RedirectMessageTo
- STEP 2: Anti-spam outbound policy
- Configure an anti-spam outbound policy:
- Navigate to Microsoft 365 Defender https://security.microsoft.com/ Expand E-mail & collaboration then select Policies & rules. Select Threat policies > Anti-spam. Select Anti-spam outbound policy (default) Click Edit protection settings Set Automatic forwarding rules dropdown to Off - Forwarding is disabled and click Save Repeat steps 4-6 for any additional higher priority, custom policies.

Confirmed composite settings:

| Setting | Required value | Microsoft surface | Remote mechanism | API/Cmdlet/CSP | Required permissions or role | License dependency | Source | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Outbound automatic forwarding mode | `Off` for no external auto-forwarding, or `Automatic` only where system-controlled forwarding is intentionally accepted | Microsoft Defender portal > Anti-spam outbound policy | Automatable | `Set-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity <PolicyName> -AutoForwardingMode Off` | Exchange Online / Defender for Office policy administrator | Exchange Online Protection / Defender for Office 365 policy surface | Configure outbound spam policies; `Set-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy` | High |
| Remote-domain automatic forwarding | `AutoForwardEnabled=$false` on the default remote domain and on any external-domain objects that should not receive forwarded mail | Exchange admin center / Exchange Online PowerShell | Automatable | `Get-RemoteDomain | Set-RemoteDomain -AutoForwardEnabled $false` after exception review | Exchange Administrator | Exchange Online | Control automatic external email forwarding from cloud mailboxes; `Set-RemoteDomain` | Medium-high |
| Mailbox SMTP forwarding | No unapproved `ForwardingAddress`, `ForwardingSmtpAddress`, or `DeliverToMailboxAndForward` forwarding remains | Exchange admin center / Exchange Online PowerShell | Automatable audit/remediation | Audit `Get-Mailbox` forwarding fields; remediate with `Set-Mailbox -ForwardingAddress $null -ForwardingSmtpAddress $null -DeliverToMailboxAndForward $false` where approved | Exchange Administrator | Exchange Online | Control automatic external email forwarding from cloud mailboxes; `Set-Mailbox` | Medium-high |
| Inbox-rule forwarding | No unapproved `ForwardTo`, `ForwardAsAttachmentTo`, or `RedirectTo` inbox rules remain | Exchange admin center / Exchange Online PowerShell | Automatable audit; remediation should be per-mailbox and change-controlled | Audit `Get-InboxRule -Mailbox <Identity>` forwarding actions; disable or remove approved malicious/unauthorized rules | Exchange Administrator / mailbox delegated audit role | Exchange Online | Control automatic external email forwarding from cloud mailboxes; Inbox rule cmdlets | Medium |
| Redirecting transport rules | No broad external redirect rules remain | Exchange admin center > Mail flow > Rules | Automatable audit/remediation | Audit `Get-TransportRule` results for non-empty `RedirectMessageTo`; remediate with `Remove-TransportRule <RuleName>` or scoped rule edits | Exchange Administrator | Exchange Online | Secure Score remediation; Exchange mail flow rule management | Medium |

Implementation note:

- Secure Score automatically monitors the outbound spam policy portion, while transport rules, inbox rules, mailbox forwarding, and remote-domain posture need separate evidence. Securityzator should show one composite control with multiple checks rather than a single "turn off forwarding" button.

- Research status: B10.1 confirmed from Microsoft Entra RBAC best-practice documentation.
- Confidence: High - Microsoft documents least privilege, PIM, access reviews, fewer than five Global Administrators, and cloud-native privileged accounts.

Required setting candidates:

- Review 'Use least privileged administrative roles' in AzureAD and apply the secure state described by Microsoft Secure Score remediation.

Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- Identify the users in your organization with a persistent global administrator role assigned. Go to Microsoft Entra ID> Roles and administrators and select the Global administrator role in the table. Identify the global admins you want to reassign to a different role. Go to Roles and administrators in Microsoft Entra ID Assign these users to roles where they can complete necessary tasks with the least amount of privilege required. For example, if a user is primarily responsible for Exchange Online administration, they should be assigned that role instead of global administrator. Be sure to have at least two global admins designated to allow for full access to the network if one of the accounts is locked out or compromised. Check out this overview of available limited administrative roles After these persistent global admins have been reassigned new roles, return to Roles and administrators and select the Global administrator role. Select the users that no longer need persistent access and then click Remove. Go to Roles and administrators in Microsoft Entra ID Emergency access accounts: If the only other global admin accounts your organization has set up are for "break-glass" scenarios, which are ineligible for role reassignment, we recommend that you set the status of this action to “Risk accepted”. Learn more about emergency access accounts

Confirmed settings:

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Persistent Global Administrator count | Fewer than five Global Administrators, while retaining at least two emergency/admin continuity accounts | Microsoft Entra admin center > Roles and administrators | Automatable audit; guided remediation | Microsoft Graph role management APIs to enumerate and adjust role assignments | Privileged Role Administrator / Global Administrator | Microsoft Entra ID; PIM requires Entra ID P2 | Best practices for Microsoft Entra roles | High |
| Least-privilege role replacement | Routine admins assigned workload-specific roles instead of Global Administrator | Microsoft Entra admin center > Roles and administrators / PIM | Automatable audit; guided remediation | Graph role assignments; PIM eligible assignments where licensed | Privileged Role Administrator | Microsoft Entra ID; Entra ID P2 for PIM | Best practices for Microsoft Entra roles; Least privileged roles by task | High |
| Recurring privileged access review | Access reviews configured for privileged roles or role-assignable groups where licensed | Microsoft Entra ID Governance / PIM | Automatable where Graph/PIM APIs are licensed; portal-guided otherwise | Access reviews / PIM APIs depending on tenant licensing | Privileged Role Administrator / Identity Governance Administrator | Microsoft Entra ID Governance / P2 | Best practices for Microsoft Entra roles | Medium-high |

Caution:

- Least privilege is governance, not just removal. Securityzator should recommend target roles per job function and preserve break-glass continuity before removing Global Administrator assignments.

Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- 1. Verify Registry Values:
- HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters\DisablePasswordChange is set to 0 or is nonexistent.
- HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\Netlogon\Parameters\MaximumPasswordAge is set to 30.
- 2. Reset Incorrect Values:
- Reset any incorrect values to their default settings.
- Check Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to ensure they do not override these settings.
- 3. If these values are correct, check if the NETLOGON service is started with sc.exe query netlogon.
- 4. Validate Password Synchronization by Running nltest /SC_VERIFY: (with DomainName being the domain NetBIOS name) can check the synchronization status and should display0 0x0 NERR_Success for both verifications.

Required setting candidates:

- Review 'Reversible passwords found in GPOs' in Azure ATP and apply the secure state described by Microsoft Secure Score remediation.

Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- In order to remove the preferences that contain passwords data, use Group Policy Management Console (GPMC) on a domain controller or from a client that has Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT) installed. You can remove any preference following these steps:
- 1.In GPMC, open the Group Policy reported in the Exposed entities tab.
- 2.Navigate to the preference configuration that contains password data and delete the object. Click Apply and OK to save your changes.
- 3.Wait a Group Policy refresh cycle to allow changes to propagate to clients (usually up to 120 minutes)
- 4.After changes are applied to all clients, delete the preference.
- 5.Repeat steps 1 through 5 as needed to clean your whole environment.
- For more information, please refer to the security advisory in the "Learn More" section.

| SYSVOL/GPO propagation residue | Clients have completed Group Policy refresh and residual password preference removed | SYSVOL / client Group Policy processing | Hybrid/on-premises action required | Wait normal GP refresh cycle, then remove remaining preference residue as needed | Domain Admin / delegated GPO editor | AD DS Group Policy | Defender for Identity Group policy security assessment | High |

- Research status: B10.16 confirmed from Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Exploit Protection and ExploitGuard Policy CSP documentation.
- Confidence: High for the deployment surface; medium for the exact tenant policy content because Securityzator needs an approved exploit-protection XML artifact before enforcing it.

Confirmed setting candidates:

- Exploit Protection Settings is configured with the tenant-approved XML policy.
- The XML contains the intended system-level mitigation states and is deployed through Intune Endpoint Security, Configuration Manager, Group Policy, PowerShell, or the ExploitGuard CSP.

Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- Within Microsoft 365 security, go to  Vulnerability management > Recommendations , read the relevant security recommendation and choose remediation or exception options.

Confirmed settings:

| Setting | Required value | Microsoft surface | Remote mechanism | API/Cmdlet/CSP | Required permissions or role | License dependency | Source | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exploit Protection XML policy | Configured XML containing tenant-approved system and application mitigation settings | Intune Endpoint Security > Attack surface reduction > Exploit Protection | Automatable through Intune policy; semi-automatable through MDM custom OMA-URI | Intune profile setting "Exploit Protection Settings"; CSP `./Device/Vendor/MSFT/Policy/Config/ExploitGuard/ExploitProtectionSettings` | Intune administrator or Graph `DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All` / endpoint security write role | Intune license for managed policy; Windows 10 1709+ for CSP | Turn on exploit protection; ExploitGuard Policy CSP | High |
| Local/export validation | Exported XML reviewed and stored as a controlled baseline artifact before tenant-wide deployment | Windows Security app / PowerShell / Configuration Manager | Device-local validation or Intune remediation for inventory | `Get-ProcessMitigation -RegistryConfigFilePath <path>` / `Set-ProcessMitigation -PolicyFilePath <path>` where local remediation is approved | Local admin or device-management execution rights | Windows endpoint support for exploit protection | Turn on exploit protection; Import, export, and deploy exploit protection configurations | Medium-high |

Implementation notes:

- Do not auto-generate mitigation XML blindly. The safe workflow is `export/reference baseline -> review compatibility -> pilot -> deploy -> collect Defender TVM evidence` because some exploit mitigations can break legacy apps.
- System-level settings can require a reboot before the device reflects the configured posture.

- Primary source: [https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?recommendationId=sca-_-scid-3001&tid=aac18d1b-e371-46d9-8d98-279d5bf85c51](https://security.microsoft.com/security-recommendations?recommendationId=sca-_-scid-3001&tid=aac18d1b-e371-46d9-8d98-279d5bf85c51)
- Research status: Confirmed remediation mapping from Microsoft service-control documentation plus Defender Vulnerability Management recommendation workflow.
- Confidence: Medium-high - Secure Score owns the recommendation; Microsoft documents the service path fields and supported service reconfiguration mechanism.

Confirmed settings:

| Setting or state | Required value | Remote mechanism | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows service executable path | If the executable path contains spaces, quote the executable portion of the service `PathName` / `binpath` while preserving arguments outside the quotes. | Intune remediation, RMM, PowerShell, or `sc.exe config <service> binpath= "<quoted exe>" <args>` after service-specific testing. | [Win32_Service `PathName`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/cimwin32prov/win32-service), [sc.exe config `binpath=`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/sc-config) |

Microsoft Secure Score remediation text:

- Within Microsoft 365 security, go to  Vulnerability management > Recommendations , read the relevant security recommendation and choose remediation or exception options.

Operational validation:

- Detection query: `Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.PathName -match '^[A-Za-z]:\\' -and $_.PathName -match '\s' -and $_.PathName -notmatch '^"' } | Select-Object Name,DisplayName,PathName`.
- Remediation must parse the executable and arguments separately. Do not wrap the full command line if arguments are present; quote only the executable path.
- Prefer a dry-run report and per-service allowlist because some vendor services self-heal, update their own path, or break if the command line is rewritten incorrectly.
